posts.title: The Open-Window Feeling, with the Window Closed
posts.excerpt: Mado Home Studio co-founders Ines Albrecht and Tomás Reyes explain how rethinking the air purifier as a windowsill object brings the fresh feeling of an open window into the calm of winter.
posts.content:
In northern Europe, there is a specific afternoon in late autumn when domestic windows close for the season. Outside, the air turns damp and grey; inside, heating radiators warm the rooms, laundry dries on racks in the hallway, and the atmosphere gradually grows dense and still. For decades, the standard response to stale indoor air has been to throw open the casement for a brief, shivering shock of cold, or to introduce a bulky plastic appliance that dominates the floor like an office photocopy machine. When we founded Mado Home Studio in Rotterdam in 2021, co-founders Ines Albrecht and Tomás Reyes began with a fundamentally different intention: to recreate the calm freshness of an open window without sacrificing the warmth and quiet of home.

The Japanese word mado translates directly to window. Historically, the windowsill is the natural threshold where architecture meets the outside world. It is where morning daylight spills across pale walls, where house plants thrive, and where the breeze enters. Yet conventional purifiers are almost always designed as floor-standing towers that block corridors and collect scuffs. We wanted Mado Air to sit gracefully on that very windowsill. Measuring 22 × 22 × 38 cm and weighing 2.6 kg, its compact square footprint with softly rounded vertical edges integrates effortlessly into window reveals and low book ledges. Wrapped in a light warm-grey woven textile developed by materials lead Léa Moreau, the purifier feels like a tactile domestic furnishing rather than an aggressive mechanical device.

Quietness is not merely a technical specification; it is an emotional necessity. Most people switch off air purifiers because the incessant drone becomes fatiguing. In our Rotterdam test room, acoustics engineer Priya Raman spent months refining internal airflow baffles to ensure Night mode operates at an extraordinary 19 dB, measured at 1 m. At 19 dB, the sound is quieter than a soft whisper in a library, allowing people like our early tester Maya Okonkwo in Lisbon to sleep peacefully with the unit right beside the bed. During daytime activities, Calm mode provides gentle, continuous circulation that leaves video calls and quiet conversations undisturbed. Even when boosted to its full 160 m³/h capacity at 28 W, sound remains capped at a gentle 46 dB.

Air filtration inside Mado Air operates through an honest, balanced mechanism. Air enters across all four lower sides through the woven fabric perimeter, passing directly through an H13-grade pleated medium paired with an activated carbon layer to capture fine particles and domestic cooking odours. Rather than distracting the eye with numeric pollution meters or flashing displays, a subtle PM2.5 light ring transitions gently from soft white to pale cyan when elevated particles are detected, returning to white as conditions clear. There are no proprietary connectivity requirements, confusing smartphone apps, or loud alert chimes. A single brushed aluminium dial on the top grille provides immediate, tactile control over every setting.

As we prepare for our initial production units to ship in March 2027, our focus remains on long-term dependability and calm living. Every unit comes backed by a 3-year warranty and a 60-day home trial overseen by test-room coordinator Hana Sato-Lindgren. Whether you place Mado Air on a wide sill in a studio flat or carry it between rooms with its tan leather loop, it is designed to restore that elusive open-window feeling to your home every single day.
